title: Apostrophes, quotation marks and dialogue
blurb: Form singular, plural and joint possessives, place marks around quotation marks the American way, and punctuate dialogue tags.
question: A student writes, “Are you ready?,” the nurse asked, and then adds, The childrens' ward is beside the mens' locker room. Each sentence breaks a rule. What are the errors, and how should each sentence read?

teach.body: Formally, an apostrophe marks a contraction or possession; quotation marks enclose a speaker's or writer's exact words and the titles of short works; dialogue punctuation separates the quoted words from the tag (she said). Plain English: US English has fixed placement rules here, and the HESI A2 tests them. Two headline rules: write the plural first and then add the possessive mark, and put periods and commas inside the closing quotation mark.

head: Job
Examples
Never
rows: Possessive pronouns: its, yours, theirs, whose
teach.caption: It's always means “it is” or “it has,” and who's means “who is.” If neither fits, write its or whose.

head: Noun
Rule
Example
rows: a day's rest, two weeks' notice
teach.caption: Write the plural first (child → children), then add the mark. Indefinite pronouns take 's too: someone's, everyone's.

Placement

teach.caption: Putting a period or comma outside the quotation mark is British style and is wrong on the HESI A2.

children.edge: The quoted words are the question
children.label: Inside
children.sub: The patient asked, “When can I go home?”

children.edge: The whole sentence is the question
children.label: Outside

teach.caption: Use only one end mark: never a question mark and a period together.

head: Pattern
Example
rows: Leah said, “My shift starts at noon.”
“My shift starts at noon,” Leah said.
“Is my shift at noon?” Leah asked.
“If you feel dizzy,” he said, “sit down.”
“I can't stay,” he said. “My bus is here.”
teach.caption: A comma links the quote and the tag. After ? or ! add no comma. The tag stays lowercase, and a split sentence resumes in lowercase. Start a new paragraph for each new speaker.

rows.label: Example
values: She asked whether it was open.

teach.caption: Capitalize the first word of a quoted full sentence. A quotation inside a quotation uses single marks: “The sign says ‘Exit only,’ so go left.”
Rule of thumb: a part goes in quotation marks; the whole it belongs to goes in italics.

teach.h: Scenario: Keisha writes a shadowing note
teach.body: Nursing applicant Keisha Morgan, shadowing on a pediatric unit, writes: The children's nurse said, “Visiting hours end at eight,” and the parents' lounge closes then. Children is an irregular plural, so it takes 's; parents ends in s, so it takes only an apostrophe. The comma after eight goes inside the closing mark, and the quote starts with a capital. Later she reports, The nurse asked whether the parents had eaten: an indirect question, so no quotation marks and a period.

teach.text: The classic HESI A2 traps: an apostrophe in a plain plural (two pen's), childrens' or mens' for irregular plurals, it's used for its, a period or comma outside the closing quotation mark (British style), a comma added after a quoted question (“Ready?,” she asked), and a capital letter where a split quotation resumes.

items: Apostrophes form contractions and possessives only, never plain plurals or possessive pronouns.
Singular: add 's. Plural in s: add '. Plural not in s: add 's. Joint ownership: last name only.
Periods and commas go inside closing quotation marks; colons and semicolons go outside.
A question mark goes inside if the quotation asks, outside if the whole sentence asks.
A comma links a quote to its tag, except after ? or !; a split quoted sentence resumes in lowercase.
Indirect quotations and questions take no quotation marks and end with a period.

summary: You can now form singular, plural, irregular, compound and joint possessives and keep apostrophes out of plain plurals. You can also place every mark correctly around closing quotation marks in US style and punctuate dialogue tags, split quotations and indirect quotations.

A.q: Which sentence follows US rules for punctuating a quotation?
options: The nurse said, “Please wait here”.
The nurse said “Please wait here.”
The nurse said, “Please wait here.”
The nurse said, “please wait here.”
A.why: A comma follows the dialogue tag, the quoted sentence is capitalized, and the period goes inside the closing mark.

whyNot.0: In US style, the period goes inside the closing quotation mark.
whyNot.1: A comma is needed to separate the tag “said” from the quotation.
whyNot.3: The first word of a quoted full sentence must be capitalized.

A.q: Which sentence about the clinic is punctuated correctly?
options: She asked whether the clinic was open?
She asked whether the clinic was open.
She asked, “whether the clinic was open.”
She asked whether, the clinic was open.
A.why: This is an indirect question: it reports what she asked, so it ends with a period and uses no quotation marks.

whyNot.0: An indirect question is a statement about a question, so it ends with a period.
whyNot.2: Quotation marks are for exact words; “whether the clinic was open” is reported speech.
whyNot.3: No comma belongs between “whether” and the rest of its clause.

A.q: The lounge is shared by all the nurses on the unit. Which sentence uses possessive forms correctly?
options: The nurses' lounge is next to the children's playroom.
The nurse's lounge is next to the children's playroom.
The nurses' lounge is next to the childrens' playroom.
The nurses's lounge is next to the children's playroom.
A.why: “Nurses” is a plural ending in s, so it adds only an apostrophe; “children” is a plural not ending in s, so it adds 's.

whyNot.1: “Nurse's” shows one owner, but the lounge belongs to all the nurses.
whyNot.2: “Children” is already plural and does not end in s, so its possessive is “children's.”
whyNot.3: A plural ending in s adds only an apostrophe, not another s.

B.q: Which sentence places the question mark correctly?
options: Did the doctor really say “no visitors”?
Did the doctor really say “no visitors?”
Did the doctor really say “no visitors.”?
Did the doctor really say, “no visitors”.
B.why: The whole sentence is the question; the quoted words are not. So the question mark goes outside.

whyNot.1: “No visitors” is not itself a question, so the question mark belongs outside.
whyNot.2: A sentence takes one end mark; the period must go.
whyNot.3: The sentence is a question, so it must end with a question mark, not a period.

B.q: Which sentence about a patient's question is punctuated correctly?
options: The patient asked, “When can I go home”?
The patient asked, “When can I go home?”.
The patient asked “When can I go home?”
The patient asked, “When can I go home?”
B.why: The quoted words are the question, so the question mark goes inside, and nothing follows it.

whyNot.0: The quotation itself is the question, so its question mark goes inside.
whyNot.1: A sentence takes one end mark; the extra period must go.
whyNot.2: A comma is needed after the dialogue tag “asked.”

B.q: Which sentence places the semicolon correctly?
options: The memo was titled “Shift Changes;” everyone read it.
The memo was titled “Shift Changes”; everyone read it.
The memo was titled “Shift Changes,” everyone read it.
The memo was titled “Shift Changes” everyone read it.
B.why: Semicolons go outside closing quotation marks.

whyNot.0: A semicolon goes outside the closing quotation mark, not inside.
whyNot.2: A comma alone between two independent clauses is a comma splice.
whyNot.3: Two independent clauses with no punctuation make a run-on.

C.q: Rosa cites an article titled Sleep and Shift Work, published in a monthly magazine called Nursing Today. How should she format the two titles?
options: Italics for the article; quotation marks for the magazine
Quotation marks for both the article and the magazine
Quotation marks for the article; italics for the magazine
Italics for both the article and the magazine
C.why: An article is a short work (quotation marks); a magazine is a long work (italics).

whyNot.0: This reverses the rule: the short work gets quotation marks and the long work gets italics.
whyNot.1: A magazine is a long work, so it takes italics.
whyNot.3: An article is a short work, so it takes quotation marks.

C.q: Which sentence correctly punctuates a quotation within a quotation?
options: Ana said, “The sign says ‘Exit only,’ so use the side door.”
Ana said, “The sign says “Exit only,” so use the side door.”
Ana said, ‘The sign says “Exit only,” so use the side door.’
Ana said, “The sign says ‘Exit only’, so use the side door.”
C.why: US style uses double marks outside and single marks inside, with the comma inside the single mark.

whyNot.1: A quotation inside a quotation uses single marks, not a second set of doubles.
whyNot.2: Single marks outside and doubles inside is British style.
whyNot.3: The comma must go inside the closing single quotation mark.

C.q: Which version of a nurse's instruction, split by a dialogue tag, is punctuated correctly?
options: “Before you stand up,” the nurse said, “Call for help.”
“Before you stand up,” the nurse said. “call for help.”
“Before you stand up”, the nurse said, “call for help.”
“Before you stand up,” the nurse said, “call for help.”
C.why: One quoted sentence is split by the tag: a comma inside the first closing mark, a comma after the tag, and the sentence resumes in lowercase.

whyNot.0: The second part continues the same sentence, so “call” is lowercase.
whyNot.1: A period after “said” would start a new sentence, but “call for help” finishes the first one, so a comma is needed.
whyNot.2: In US style the comma goes inside the closing quotation mark.

reteach.title: Quotation marks are a fence
reteach.question: Think of quotation marks as a fence around someone's exact words. In the US, which pieces of punctuation live inside the fence, and which stay outside?

blocks.h: Small pets inside, big furniture outside
blocks.body: In US style, the little marks, periods and commas, always go inside the fence, even when they don't seem to belong to the quote. The bigger marks, colons and semicolons, always stay outside. Question marks and exclamation points are visitors: they go inside if they belong to the person speaking, and outside if they belong to the whole sentence. The apostrophe is a name tag on the owner: put it on the owner's whole name as written, nurses' for many nurses, children's for many children.

blocks.text: British books put periods and commas outside the fence. The HESI A2 uses US rules, so “Wait here”. is wrong and “Wait here.” is right.

explain.body: Use an apostrophe for missing letters (they're = they are) or possession (nurses' station). Plain plurals and possessive pronouns take none.

test.q: Which sentence about the nurses uses apostrophes correctly?
options: The nurse's are sure they're ready.
The nurses are sure their ready.
The nurses' are sure they're ready.
The nurses are sure they're ready.
test.why: Nurses is a plain plural (no apostrophe), and they're means “they are.”

whyNot.0: Nurses is a plain plural here, so it takes no apostrophe.
whyNot.1: “They are ready” is meant, so the contraction they're is needed.
whyNot.2: Nothing belongs to the nurses, so no possessive apostrophe.

explain.body: Singular nouns add 's; plurals ending in s add only an apostrophe; plurals not ending in s add 's. Time and money expressions follow the same rules: one day's pay, two weeks' notice.

test.q: Which sentence about a resignation is written correctly?
options: She gave two week's notice before leaving the clinic.
She gave two weeks notice before leaving the clinic.
She gave two weeks' notice before leaving the clinic.
She gave two weeks's notice before leaving the clinic.
test.why: “Two weeks” is a plural ending in s, so the possessive adds only an apostrophe: two weeks' notice.

whyNot.0: “Week's” is singular, but there are two weeks.
whyNot.1: The notice belongs to the two weeks, so the possessive apostrophe is needed.
whyNot.3: A plural ending in s adds only an apostrophe, not 's.

explain.body: In US style, periods and commas always go inside closing quotation marks. Colons and semicolons always go outside.

test.q: Which sentence quoting a medication label is punctuated correctly?
options: “Take one tablet daily,” the label says.
“Take one tablet daily”, the label says.
“Take one tablet daily.” the label says.
“Take one tablet daily” the label says.
test.why: A comma ends the quoted sentence when a tag follows, and in US style it goes inside the closing mark.

whyNot.1: In US style the comma goes inside the closing quotation mark.
whyNot.2: When the sentence continues with a tag, the quote ends with a comma, not a period.
whyNot.3: A comma is needed to separate the quotation from the tag.

explain.body: Ask who is asking. If the quoted words are a question, the mark goes inside. If the whole sentence is the question, it goes outside, and the quote's own period disappears.

test.q: Which question about the lab places its question mark correctly?
options: Who said, “The lab is closed?”
Who said, “The lab is closed.”?
Who said, “The lab is closed”?
Who said “The lab is closed?”.
test.why: The whole sentence asks the question, and the quoted words are a statement, so the question mark goes outside.

whyNot.0: The quoted words are a statement, not a question, so the mark goes outside.
whyNot.1: A sentence takes one end mark; the quote's period is dropped.
whyNot.3: The question mark is on the wrong side and an extra period is added.

explain.body: A comma links a quotation to its tag (she said), and the tag stays lowercase. When the quotation ends with a question mark or an exclamation point, no comma is added before the tag.

test.q: Which sentence punctuates the dialogue tag correctly?
options: “Are you feeling dizzy?,” the nurse asked.
“Are you feeling dizzy?” the nurse asked.
“Are you feeling dizzy,” the nurse asked.
“Are you feeling dizzy?” The nurse asked.
test.why: The quoted question ends with its own question mark inside the closing mark, no comma is added, and the tag continues in lowercase.

whyNot.0: No comma is added after a question mark that ends a quotation.
whyNot.2: The quoted words are a question, so they need a question mark, not a comma.
whyNot.3: The tag continues the same sentence, so “the” is lowercase.
